sense.text: Christ went into the synagogue at Nazareth on the Sabbath and stood up to read. Esaias is Isaiah; the portion he opened is Isaiah 61. The gospel is good tidings, good news, or glad tidings, and Christ announces that news from the prophets.

The poor, brokenhearted, captives, blind, and bruised are our people. These conditions describe the people who need liberation, not a people already enjoying freedom and dominion. Black people, together with the other scattered tribes identified among Hispanics, Native Americans, and the islands, must recognize themselves in this promise.

Church teaching can leave a person unable to see himself in the scripture. The words must be examined one by one in Isaiah 61 so that healing, liberty, and the acceptable year retain their connection to Israel's condition.
Christ identifies himself as the fulfilment of the scripture he has just read. The mission described by Isaiah is his mission; Luke and Isaiah are speaking about the same deliverance.

Good tidings means the gospel. Its recipients are the meek: people who humble themselves and submit to God's will. Meekness does not mean being soft, accepting foolishness, or lacking strength. It is strength under God's control, with patience, concern for others, and trust in his justice. Moses is the example of submission to that will.

The brokenhearted have been crushed by grief and loss and need God to restore them. This includes spiritual poverty, repentance, and humility, but also the condition of our people after slavery and oppression. Telling a dispossessed people to pull themselves up by their bootstraps ignores that their resources were taken from them. The gospel promises an end to that sorrow.

Captivity includes literal capture, enslavement, and removal into other countries. It cannot be reduced to a feeling or applied as though every nation occupied the same position. Israel sinned, was delivered to enemies, and must remember who they are, confess their wickedness, and return to God. The same God who allowed captivity promises to end it.

The prison is both physical and spiritual. America and the other countries of the dispersion hold our people under foreign rule; the ghettos and their conditions have become so familiar that many no longer recognize the confinement. Removing chains did not return Israel to its own land or put Israel under its own laws. Blindness includes not knowing this condition.

Being bound also includes being held by sin. A comfortable income or a good job does not cancel the nation's captivity. Liberty through Christ must address both the sin that brought the bondage and the bondage itself.

precepts.why:
Moses illustrates meekness as humility and submission to God. His leadership was not weakness: he relied on God and submitted to God's will. The example corrects the idea that the meek are merely timid people who let others do whatever they want.

The strength needed to lead Israel belongs under God's control. That is the character required of those receiving the good tidings.

The meek inherit the land and receive the abundance promised by God. Humility and obedience do not leave Israel permanently dispossessed; they lead toward the inheritance.

This is the reward attached to meekness, not an instruction to accept captivity as Israel's final condition.

The meek who receive the blessing are those who submit themselves to God's will. Their inheritance of the earth agrees with Isaiah's good tidings to the meek.

Christ's blessing therefore carries the same promise of an inheritance for the obedient, rather than making meekness another name for weakness.

The Lamb feeds his people and leads them to living fountains of waters, and God wipes away all their tears. The brokenhearted are not promised endless crying with no remedy. Christ supplies what they lack and brings their grief to an end.

This is the completion of the healing announced in Isaiah: the people whose oppression has made them mourn receive care and comfort from God.

God removes death, sorrow, crying, and pain. The former things include the captivity, poverty, and oppression that have made our people brokenhearted.

The promise is a change in their actual condition. These causes of mourning pass away; the people are not simply taught to endure the same suffering forever.

Falling by the sword and being led captive into all nations explains the captives of Isaiah 61. Rome's destruction in AD 70 began the scattering under discussion, and captivity continued through the countries of the dispersion, including Spain, France, Britain, and America.

Jerusalem remains trodden down until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. The verse therefore describes both the conquest and an extended period of foreign dominion. Liberty must reverse that condition.

Sin brings God's anger, defeat before enemies, and captivity in countries far away or nearby. The people must bethink themselves in those lands: remember who they are as the twelve tribes, acknowledge their sin, and make supplication.

Repentance is not simply demanding release while continuing in wickedness. Israel must confess having done wrong and return to the God whose commandments were broken. This explains how literal captivity and spiritual correction belong together in the promise of liberty.

God directs the work of building his city and releasing his captives. Their release is not purchased for a price or granted in exchange for a reward.

The emphasis is on God's declared purpose to let his captives go. Isaiah's liberty is a real release of people who have been held, not merely a change of attitude inside their captivity.

Even mighty captors cannot prevent the promised deliverance. Assyria and Babylon were terrible powers in their time; America, Spain, Portugal, and Europe occupy that position in the application to the present captivity. Israel is the prey, and God undertakes to contend with those who contend against Israel and to save their children.

The judgment on the oppressors is severe, involving their own flesh and blood. The conclusion identifies the Saviour and Redeemer as the mighty One of Jacob. This is a promise directed to Jacob's children, not a description that treats oppressor and oppressed as the same people.

Israel must seek God with the whole heart. God promises to be found, turn their captivity, gather them from the nations and places where they were driven, and return them.

The order matters: wholehearted seeking and repentance belong with the gathering. The promise concerns scattered people being brought back, confirming the literal meaning of liberty to the captives.

The help comes from the God of Jacob, the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them. He keeps truth, executes judgment for the oppressed, gives food to the hungry, and looses the prisoners.

The opening identification keeps the prisoners connected to Jacob. Hunger includes the need for physical food and for spiritual nourishment. Loosing the prisoners belongs to the same work of justice and restoration as feeding and defending the oppressed.

The passage calls the ruler a man: the king of Babylon, rather than an invisible being detached from earthly power. The application identifies Lucifer with the white imperial power that makes the earth tremble, shakes kingdoms, destroys cities, and refuses to open the house of its prisoners.

America is treated as that prison house. Wars and the destruction of other countries show the reach of the ruling power. Dividing African people from Black Americans, including disputes over nationality and identity, keeps people from recognizing a shared captivity. The promise in Isaiah 61 answers the ruler's refusal to release his prisoners.

Opening blind eyes and bringing prisoners out of darkness explains the prison language in Isaiah 61. The blindness is spiritual as well as the confinement being physical: people can live under foreign rule without recognizing that they remain captive.

An end to visible chains is not the same as returning to one's own land and laws. The countries where Israel is scattered remain the places of imprisonment from which deliverance is promised.

The blood of the covenant is Christ's death on the cross. Through it the prisoners are sent out of the pit. The pit is America and the other countries where Israel is scattered; the absence of water is the absence of truth. The stronghold to which the prisoners of hope must turn is the Bible.

The promise goes beyond relief inside the pit. Judah is bent as the bow, Ephraim fills it, and the remaining sons of Zion are raised against Greece. Israel is made like the sword of a mighty man. This is treated as a future event, not something already completed. Covenant deliverance restores the people who had been prisoners.

Ephraim's iniquity is bound up and his sin is hid. Being bound therefore includes the sin holding the people, not only the visible restrictions imposed by captors.

This leads into Christ's explanation in John 8: freedom from sin and freedom from bondage must be understood together. Wealth does not remove either national captivity or responsibility for sin.

sense.text: The truth makes Israel free in both a spiritual and a literal sense. Freedom from sin and freedom from captivity are connected, not competing explanations of Christ's words.

The wealthy men answered as Abraham's seed and denied having been in bondage. They overlooked Rome's dominion and yearly taxation because their own lives were comfortable. Personal prosperity can blind a person to the captivity of his people.

“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” Christ brings out the spiritual side, but that does not remove the literal side. Breaking God's commandments brought Israel into captivity. Serving sin produces the bondage from which the people need deliverance.
The Son's freedom is freedom from sin and freedom from bondage. Both belong to the promise; the men arguing with Christ failed to recognize that connection.

precepts.why:
The curses follow refusal to hear God and keep his commandments and statutes. Among those curses, sons and daughters are given to another people, parents long for them without power to recover them, and children go into captivity rather than being enjoyed by their parents.

That is slavery as a result of sin. These verses join the spiritual servitude of John 8 to the literal bondage of the nation: disobedience is the cause, and captivity is one of its consequences. Christ's promise of freedom must address both.

sense.text:
The acceptable year includes “the day of vengeance of our God”. God has an appointed time to answer the captivity and oppression described in verse 1. Vengeance is retribution for wrongdoing and an act of justice; comfort for those who mourn is connected to that judgment, not separated from it.

Vengeance begins with the Lord. Christ first breaks the armies of the world, and Israel then has the part God gives them. The commentaries must be tested against the scriptures rather than accepted when they erase that part.

Mourning is deep sorrow over the condition and losses of the people. Families asking for justice after the deaths of their children illustrate that grief. The promised comfort is deliverance, return, and an end to the causes of mourning. Israel must remain faithful while waiting for God to act.

precepts.why:
God lays his vengeance on Edom by the hand of his people Israel. This corrects the claim that divine vengeance excludes any role for Israel. It starts with the Lord, and the people act in the role and order he appoints.

Christ first defeats the opposing armies. Israel's subsequent part agrees with the earlier picture of Judah, Ephraim, and Zion made into a weapon in Zechariah 9. The vengeance is God's, including when he executes it through his people.

God lifts his hand to heaven, declares that he lives for ever, and prepares judgment. To whet the sword is to sharpen it. The sword and arrows repay enemies and those who hate him, with blood marking the severity of that repayment.

The conclusion joins vengeance for the blood of his servants to mercy for his land and people. Judgment on their enemies and mercy toward Israel are not opposites here: they are the two sides of the promised deliverance.

The Lord has a day of vengeance and a year of recompences for Zion's controversy. Recompence is payback. This is the same appointed vengeance announced in Isaiah 61.

The controversy concerns who the Israelites are and whose land it is. The promise answers those disputes with God's judgment rather than leaving them unresolved forever.

Weak hands and feeble knees must be strengthened. Fearful hearts are told to be strong because God will come with vengeance and recompence to save them. The expectation of justice is meant to steady obedience, not make people abandon the truth.

That applies to remaining faithful in marriage, rejecting adultery, maintaining modest dress, and not letting discouragement turn into rebellion. Strength means continuing to do what God requires while deliverance has not yet arrived.

The ransomed return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy; sorrow and sighing flee away. This is a real contrast to present grief, war, and the pressure of bills. Vengeance brings salvation and lasting comfort to those waiting for God.

The figure coming from Edom and Bozrah is Christ. Bozrah is identified as Edom's capital. His glorious clothing is stained red because he has trodden his enemies as grapes in a winepress.

He treads alone at this stage: no man of the people assists him in this initial overthrow. The blood on his garments expresses the fierceness of that judgment. The day of vengeance in his heart is also the year of his redeemed.

This is why the passage is not treated as a history of an Edom that has simply vanished. The vengeance and the deliverance of Israel are still expected, and they explain the acceptable year in Isaiah 61.

The New Testament also calls it righteous for God to repay tribulation to those who trouble his people. Recompense means pay back. The trouble is traced beyond individual offenders in the community to the system that shaped their environment, including ghettos and redlining. The comparison with They Cloned Tyrone and the discussion of behavioural-sink experiments illustrate the argument that destructive behaviour is cultivated by oppressive conditions.

Those who are troubled are invited to rest with the believers in the scriptures. They first have to recognize that they are a troubled people in need of that comfort. Rest does not erase the promised judgment: Christ is revealed from heaven with mighty angels and flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God or obey the gospel.

Edom and those following him are included in that opposition. Everlasting destruction answers the tribulation, while Christ is glorified in his saints, identified as Israel. This connects the gospel's comfort directly to Isaiah's day of vengeance rather than treating vengeance as absent from the New Testament.

Enemies open their mouths against the people, and fear, a snare, desolation, and destruction produce continual tears. Jeremiah's weeping over the destruction of the daughter of his people gives a concrete picture of mourning.

The tears continue until the Lord looks down from heaven. Israel's sorrow is not an abstraction; it is grief over a people in ruin. Seeing images of that suffering hurts and can bring tears, but it is not permission to jump up and take action against people. Israel has to wait for the Lord's return. The comfort promised in Isaiah answers that grief, and its end depends on God's intervention.

The people in Zion at Jerusalem will weep no more, and God answers the voice of their cry. The bread of adversity is hardship; the water of affliction is their tears. Their present distress is not the final state promised to them.

Teachers will no longer be hidden. The classes and the teachers bringing out the word in the streets are part of that application: people can see and hear instruction that redirects them. The word behind them identifies the right way when they turn to the right or left, calling them away from false religions and back to obedience.

The redeemed return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy. Gladness replaces sorrow and mourning.

The destination is a return to the land, and the change is a lasting end to the grief of captivity. This directly explains the comfort promised to those who mourn in Isaiah 61.

sense.text:
The promise is appointed to “them that mourn in Zion”. Zion is the twelve tribes of Israel, identifying the people addressed by the gospel rather than making the promise indiscriminately about everyone on the planet.

Beauty replaces ashes, joy replaces mourning, and praise replaces the heavy spirit. Our people's grief includes families mourning deaths and violence and those who remain imprisoned or forgotten. The examples of bereaved families and Black political prisoners keep the promise connected to the conditions of a people, not only an individual's mood.

Those same afflicted people are to become trees of righteousness, God's planting for his glory. Their present humiliation is not their promised end.

The people expected the kingdom to appear immediately. They thought Christ would destroy Rome and bring the day of vengeance then. That expectation explains why the parable is given: the first coming and the final overthrow of the captors must not be collapsed into one moment.

precepts.why:
The apostles ask whether Christ will restore the kingdom to Israel at that time. The question identifies both their expectation of restoration and the people whose kingdom it is.

They were still looking for the timing of Israel's deliverance, not asking when a kingdom belonging equally to every nation would appear. This is the same expectation of immediate restoration behind Luke 19.

John sends from prison to ask whether Christ is the one to come. He had spoken boldly to Herod about having his brother's wife and was now confined, while expecting the promised deliverer to release the captives. His question concerns that expectation and its timing.

Christ points to the works being done: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor receive the gospel. The blessing on those not offended in him encourages John despite his present imprisonment. This was the time for Christ's sacrifice, not yet the time for the vengeance and national deliverance everyone wanted.

John's question does not make him wicked. The immediate overthrow and release he expected had not happened, but the works still testified to Christ's identity.

sense.text: Christ calls John the Baptist greater than anyone born of women. Calling John wicked contradicts that testimony. The least in the kingdom is greater because the kingdom brings a condition of righteousness without the fear and sin that remain in the present life.

The kingdom suffering violence is Israel on earth, not a battle occurring up in the sky. Rome took Jerusalem by force under Pompey around 63 BC, establishing the dominion under which the people later paid taxes to Caesar. The violent power is Rome; Israel is the kingdom being subjected to violence.

Christ reveals John the Baptist as Elias, Elijah who was to come. Receiving that identification requires ears to hear it. John's question from prison must be understood alongside Christ's recognition of him, not used to discredit him.

precepts.why:
After John the Baptist had been killed, Christ was transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and Moses and Elias appeared talking with him. Elias is connected to the identification Christ had already given of John the Baptist.

Christ knew his own crucifixion was approaching. The appearance of Moses and Elias with him reinforces John's standing and answers the accusation that John was wicked. The apostle John who witnessed the transfiguration is not being confused with John the Baptist who had died.

sense.text: The kingdom was not going to appear immediately. The coming of Christ and the gathering of Israel require events that had not yet occurred, including the fall and captivity of all twelve tribes.
The nobleman is Christ, and the far country is heaven. He departs to receive a kingdom and will return. His absence does not cancel the promise or mean the servants may stop working.

The servants are Israelites. The pounds are money in the parable, representing the precious understanding of God's commandments entrusted to them. “Occupy till I come” requires using that understanding and doing the work while Christ is away.

The citizens who hated Christ include the elders, chief priests, and scribes who rejected him. Their rejection must not be turned into a claim that every Israelite rejected Christ. They did not want his rule.

Receiving the kingdom involves war and the overthrow of opposing powers; it is not a peaceful handover from those currently ruling. After receiving it, Christ calls the servants to account for what they did with the understanding he gave them. Every man and woman must answer for their work.

The faithful servant multiplied what was given to him and receives authority over ten cities. The cities are real responsibility, not an empty compliment. Governing them requires teaching and enforcing God's moral, civil, ceremonial, and dietary laws.

Ruling even a household can be difficult; ruling cities will not be an easy task. People accustomed to other ways will resist being corrected. Faithfulness in the present small responsibility prepares a servant for much greater authority.

The second servant also increased what he received, gaining five pounds. Different servants produce different amounts, but the point remains productive use of what was entrusted to each rather than burying it.

The pound laid up in a napkin represents a gift or understanding left unused. Excuses do not turn inactivity into obedience. God's business requires fervent service, and fruitlessness brings removal rather than approval.

Austere means stern, cold in appearance or manner, somber, grave, and morally strict. Christ was a cold brother. The servant knew the character of his lord but used that knowledge as an excuse. Christ is away, so his servants must labour; he returns to receive the increase of the work they were meant to do.
The wicked servant is judged out of his own mouth. Knowing the Lord's strictness should have prompted obedience, not inactivity. God's mercy for his own name does not make corrupt conduct acceptable.

The bank is the congregation, where a person's gift can be put to work and produce an increase. Each person should serve according to the ability and understanding actually given to him. Teach what you know instead of pretending to understand a difficult passage you cannot explain.

Age and disability affect the kind of work a person can do, but do not make every contribution impossible. Even brothers using wheelchairs can hand out flyers. The point is to use the capacity one has rather than make excuses for leaving the gift idle.

precepts.why:
Paul addresses Christ's coming and the gathering together to him. The believers must not be shaken by claims, messages, or supposed letters announcing that the day is already at hand. The falling away and the revealing of the man of sin must happen first.

The falling away is applied to all twelve tribes falling into captivity. Judah, Benjamin, Levi, and remnants of the others were still in the land at that time; Rome's overthrow in AD 70 still lay ahead. The man of sin is identified with the white ruling power being exposed for what it is.

This answers the expectation in Luke 19. Deliverance was not immediate, because the intervening fall, captivity, and revelation had not all taken place.

Christ is taken up and a cloud receives him out of the disciples' sight. His ascent supplies the meaning of the nobleman's journey to a far country.

That country is heaven, the true heavenly habitation, not another earthly province. He has gone there and is to return, leaving work for his servants in the interval.

Israel is named as God's servant, Jacob whom he has chosen, the seed of Abraham. This identifies the servants in the parable.

The charge to occupy is given within that relationship: Israel receives understanding from the Lord and is responsible for what is done with it.

The children of Israel are God's servants, whom he brought out of Egypt. The identification is explicit and agrees with Isaiah's naming of Israel as the servant.

The servants entrusted with the pounds are therefore understood as Israel, not an undefined collection of people with no connection to the covenant or the Exodus.

God's commandments are loved above gold, even fine gold. That comparison explains why money represents something more precious than ordinary currency in the parable.

The pounds are the understanding of God's commandments. Their value demands that the servants put them to use rather than hide them.

Christ identifies the elders, chief priests, and scribes as those who reject him. The named leadership clarifies the citizens who hate the nobleman and reject his rule.

Their opposition must not be expanded into an accusation that all Israel rejected Christ. The distinction matters when identifying his enemies in the parable.

The Lord comes with fire and chariots, rendering anger and rebuke and pleading by fire and sword. Many are slain. Receiving the kingdom therefore involves judgment and war, not simply arriving to take an uncontested throne.

The gardens are applied to false churches, and the eating of swine and other unclean foods is included among the practices judged. The return requires the destruction of opposing powers and disobedience before the kingdom's government is established.

Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels. The opposing forces are applied to Satan's armies among America, Europe, China, and Russia. They do not prevail, and the deceiver and accuser are cast down.

Only then comes the announcement of salvation, strength, the kingdom of God, and the power of his Christ. The order explains the nobleman returning after receiving the kingdom: victory over the opposition precedes the kingdom's establishment.

Labour is directed toward being accepted by Christ. Everyone must appear before his judgment seat to receive for what was done in the body, whether good or bad.

That is the accounting represented by calling the servants and asking what they gained. The responsibility includes women as well as men; no one is exempt from answering for the use of what God gave them.

Each person gives account of himself to God. A servant cannot make someone else's conduct answer for his own.

Christ's return therefore brings an individual reckoning of work and obedience, just as the nobleman asks each servant what his pound has gained.

Faithfulness in little shows faithfulness in much, while injustice in little also exposes injustice in much. Present service is the test for greater responsibility.

The servant's handling of one pound is not too small to matter. The way he uses it shows whether he can be trusted with the authority represented by the cities.

The one who overcomes and keeps Christ's works to the end receives power over the nations and rules them with a rod of iron. The image of breaking a potter's vessels describes firm rule, not a government that leaves resistance untouched.

This explains the authority over cities in Luke 19. Nations accustomed to their own practices will have to learn God's laws. Such authority is serious work and requires the faithfulness being tested now.

The person who has is given more and receives abundance; the person who has not loses even what he has. The successful servants' increase introduces that principle.

The second part points ahead to the idle servant. The difference is not simply how much each began with, but whether what was entrusted was put to use.

Service to the Lord must not be slothful. Fervency of spirit belongs in God's business.

The napkin represents the opposite: possessing a gift while refusing to work with it. Diligence is an obligation, not an optional enthusiasm for a few people.

The branch that bears no fruit is taken away, while the branch that bears fruit is purged to bring forth more. Fruitlessness is treated as removal and death, not a safe way to preserve one's place.

Trials that purge a productive person are different from the judgment on someone who refuses to produce anything. The servant with the unused pound should not mistake inactivity for safety.

The sinner will not be reproved and finds an excuse according to his own will. That is the attitude behind leaving the pound in a napkin.

An explanation for doing nothing can conceal refusal to accept correction. The servant must examine his own will rather than expect excuses to count as the work Christ commanded.

God deals with the house of Israel for his name's sake rather than according to their wicked ways and corrupt doings. Their continued opportunity comes from mercy, not because those ways are righteous.

That mercy does not make the Lord indulgent toward the idle servant. He is still the austere Lord before whom corrupt conduct and self-justifying words are judged.

Gifts differ according to the grace given, and prophecy is exercised according to the proportion of faith. Each servant must work within the understanding and ability he actually possesses.

Someone who understands Deuteronomy 28 can teach it without pretending to understand 2 Esdras 12. The congregation has room for different useful contributions. Even age or physical limitation does not justify refusing every task that remains possible.

sense.text: The great house is the twelve tribes of Israel. Gold and silver represent vessels of honour, while wood and earth illustrate those bringing dishonour, including the servant who hides his gift and makes excuses. Being in the house does not mean everyone is behaving honourably.

A person must purge himself from dishonourable influences to be useful to the Master. Examine the circle around you: are those men or women helping you or bringing you down? Separation from harmful company is part of becoming a vessel of honour.

The example from New York in the early 1990s is repeatedly getting into trouble with brothers who wanted the clubs and 42nd Street after class, then choosing better company. The warning about being surrounded by a-holes is blunt: get away from people who keep drawing you into trouble. Merely calling those people brothers did not make their influence good.

Women also have to examine circles built on gossip or disrespect toward husbands. Companionship should support obedience, not make foolishness seem normal. Being sanctified and fit for the Master's use requires a real change in those influences.

precepts.why:
The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour, but the way of the wicked seduces people. Keeping harmful company in the belief that you will surely change everyone else ignores that warning.

The wicked person's way can draw the righteous away instead. This explains the need to purge oneself from a destructive circle rather than keep supplying excuses for it.

sense.text: Usury here is the interest or increase expected on what was entrusted. The bank is the congregation, where resources and gifts support the work. Even if a servant does not carry out every task himself, he can put what he has where it contributes to an increase.

The unused pound is taken from the unproductive servant and given to the one with ten. The objection that he already has ten does not change the rule: those who use what they receive gain more, while the idle lose what they had.

The additional pound is connected to additional authority: the responsibility the idle servant would have received goes to the faithful one. The servants' different gains correspond to different responsibilities, not an equal reward for unequal faithfulness.

The enemies who refuse Christ's reign face death before him. This is the same austere ruler described earlier, not a ruler who approves continued rebellion.

The next question is who those enemies are among Israel today. Opposition to the gospel matters, but the possibility of repentance must also be understood; that question leads into Romans 11.

precepts.why:
Those who owned lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles, and distribution was made according to need. Here the money and property are literal, unlike the understanding represented by the pound in the parable.

The example shows resources placed in the congregation to support the work and those doing it, including the needs of workers' families. It is not presented as a reward for refusing to work. Contributing what one has can help the body produce the increase Christ expects.

The same rule is read again at the point where the pound is removed: the one who has receives more, and the one who has not loses even what he has.

The faithful servant's existing increase is the reason he receives another responsibility, not a reason to withhold it. The idle servant's unused gift and the authority connected to it are transferred to someone who has shown himself productive.

sense.text: The Deliverer out of Zion is Christ. His covenant turns away ungodliness from Jacob and takes away their sins. Israel's salvation is connected to that removal of sin, not to permission to remain wicked.

Those among our people who disbelieve and follow other religions are enemies concerning the gospel. In Paul's time, the opposing scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees illustrated that position. Present opposition to the teaching is applied in the same way.

Being beloved for the fathers' sakes does not mean their opposition is acceptable merely because they are Israelites. The essential point is that they can still repent. Paul himself was an enemy of the gospel before being allowed to turn. The same possibility remains for brothers and sisters now fighting the teaching.

The prayer is that they wake up, admit they were wrong, and repent. Their current hostility and the hope of their repentance must both be kept in view.

Christ did not wait for these people to repent before dying for them. He died first, while their repentance would come later. The gifts and calling therefore provide an opportunity before the sinner has yet turned, rather than proving that repentance is unnecessary.

The just are our people, and the wicked plotting against them include the nations and Israelites who join those nations against the truth. Gnashing with the teeth includes speaking evil against the people and denying their identity.

Arguments insisting that our people are only Africans or Hamites, or changing the description of Christ to avoid admitting he is Black, illustrate that opposition. The discussion of competing editions and claims about an Israelite history book is presented as another example of crafty counsel aimed at undermining the teaching.
The Lord laughs because he sees the wicked person's day coming. The apparent success of the plot does not mean it will escape judgment.

The drawn sword is war, and the bow is aimed at the poor and needy. These are the same afflicted people addressed in Isaiah 61 and Luke 4. Upright conversation is conduct governed by the Bible. The opposition is directed against both the people and the righteous way they are being taught.

precepts.why:
The heathen rage and the rulers take counsel together against the Lord and his anointed. Christ and Israel are connected with that opposition. Breaking the bands and casting away the cords is applied to breaking up the schools, the tribes, and their teaching.

The one in heaven laughs and holds the plotters in derision, then answers in wrath. That agrees with Psalm 37: the Lord sees beyond the counsel being assembled to the judgment that is coming upon those assembling it.

sense.text: Enemies concerning the gospel can repent and are beloved in that sense. The warning remains real for those who will not turn. Opposition to Christ is not harmless merely because the opponent belongs to Israel.

precepts.why:
Sinning against Christ wrongs one's own soul, and those who hate him love death. Rejecting the gospel harms the person doing the rejecting.

The opportunity to repent in Romans 11 must not be mistaken for immunity from judgment. Continuing in hatred leaves the person on the side of death.

sense.text: Refusing God's statutes and judgments and polluting his Sabbaths identifies rebellion against him. Israel's own children acted as enemies through that disobedience, and God's fury met them in the wilderness.

God rules with a mighty hand, a stretched-out arm, and fury poured out. This is the same strict rule represented by the austere nobleman in Luke 19. Deliverance does not give Israel permission to reject that rule.

The gathering is of Israel out of the peoples and countries where they are scattered. It is not a promise to gather every nation into the same identity. The power that brings them out belongs to the same Lord who judges rebellion.

The gathering leads first to the wilderness, where the Lord pleads with the people face to face. They are going back to the wilderness of Egypt, the same setting in which the fathers were corrected. They are not taken straight into the land with no further dealing.

Face-to-face instruction will answer things now understood only partly. Questions about details of the future kingdom should not be filled with inventions while those answers have not been given. The old wilderness history is an example for the generation that will face this dealing again.

Passing under the rod and entering the bond of the covenant involves strict government. The present opportunity to repent should not be treated as endless permission to sin. Adultery and theft are used as examples of conduct that will not be dismissed with an apology in that future judgment.

Some rebels are brought out of the countries only to be purged in the wilderness and never enter the land of Israel. Being delivered out of a country is therefore not proof that the person has completed the journey or will be allowed into the land.

Rebels can be men, women, or children. This is connected to the enemies in Luke 19 who refuse Christ's reign. Christ establishes order, including appointed leaders, and rebellion against that order is not excused by demanding to hear directly from him. The example of Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the elders warns against repeating the same refusal to listen.

The wilderness is a place of instruction and judgment before entry. Israel must learn from the fathers' failures now instead of expecting national deliverance to cancel the need for obedience.

precepts.why:
Seeing through a glass darkly is the present partial understanding through the Bible; face-to-face understanding is still to come. The promise in Ezekiel supplies that future setting for direct instruction.

Questions about details not yet made known, including life during the thousand years, should wait for Christ's answer. Partial knowledge is not authority to invent explanations.

Paul calls the people who passed under the cloud and through the sea the fathers of those he addresses. That is used to identify the Corinthians as Israelites. The common baptism unto Moses, spiritual food and drink, and the Rock identified as Christ show that the Son was dealing with Israel in the Exodus.

Many were nevertheless overthrown in the wilderness. Idolatry, fornication, tempting Christ, and murmuring brought judgment. The twenty-three thousand who fell, the serpents, and the destroyer are not stories detached from the present responsibility of Israel.

The repeated word examples is the point. Those events were written for the admonition of the people upon whom the ends of the world are come. The application is to the generation that will again be brought to that wilderness. Israel must learn the lesson before repeating the fathers' rebellion there.

The Lord destroys the tongue of the Egyptian sea and smites the river into seven streams so that people can go over dryshod. This is connected to the future return through Egypt.

As the earlier Exodus included a miraculous crossing, the coming deliverance also involves God's removal of the barrier. It supports taking Ezekiel's wilderness of Egypt as a real stage of the return rather than only a figure of speech.

The fountain opened to the house of David and Jerusalem is connected to Christ's cleansing from sin and uncleanness. Idols, false prophets, and the unclean spirit are removed from the land.

The passage then gives the severe example of parents judging a child who prophesies lies in the Lord's name. This illustrates the rebels mentioned in Ezekiel: children as well as adults can oppose the order being established. The connection is to the future purging, not an assurance that everyone brought out of captivity enters the land.

The warning agrees with the wilderness examples in 1 Corinthians 10. Deliverance and covenant cleansing do not protect continued falsehood and rebellion from judgment.

sense.text: The fathers named by God are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. These are the fathers of the biblical church, rather than later religious authorities offered as substitutes for them.
The prophet raised up like Moses comes from the brethren of the children of Israel. That prophet is Christ, whom Israel must hear.

The church in the wilderness is the twelve tribes with Moses. The identity of that assembly answers the claim that the biblical church is a later denomination. The other nations present are described here as Israel's slaves, not as changing the identity of the church.

Baptist, Pentecostal, and Catholic institutions are rejected as replacements for that biblical assembly. The answer must come from the people actually named in the scripture.

Christ warns that people will come in his name and deceive many. The application is to Europeans replacing Black images with their own images of Christ. Claiming Christ's name does not itself establish that the representation is true; the warning requires testing the claim.

The power making war on the saints is identified with the white conquering power. The saints are the children of Israel, whom that power overcomes before extending dominion over kindreds, tongues, and nations.

The conquest is connected to religious representation: the ruler who subdues peoples also spreads the image they are taught to worship.

Worldwide worship is connected to the conquering power's reach, while those written in the Lamb's book of life are distinguished from it. The discussion of a European image and the claim about Cesare Borgia as its model illustrates the argument that the conqueror's image was presented as Christ. Accepting that image is treated as part of the deception, not as proof of the image's truth.

precepts.why:
The saints are explicitly identified as the children of Israel. That naming supplies the identity of the people against whom war is made in Revelation 13.

The designation is not extended here to Edomites, Philistines, or Moabites. The connection keeps the conquest of the saints tied to the conquest of Israel.

sense.text:
The children of sinners can inherit reproach for the ungodliness of their fathers. The answer to disclaiming any connection with a forefather's oppression is that descendants can still be direct beneficiaries of what those forefathers did.

The inherited benefit and the inherited reproach are brought together. The children complaining about an ungodly father illustrates why that history is not erased simply by belonging to a later generation.

precepts.why:
The judgment on the children is stated in connection with the iniquity of their fathers, preventing them from rising, possessing the land, and filling the world with cities. It is paired with Ecclesiasticus to show a biblical example of consequences extending to posterity.

The application concerns descendants continuing to benefit from the power and possessions produced by their forefathers' wrongdoing. The severity is presented as the Lord's judgment in the passage, not as a conclusion based only on a personal grievance.

sense.text:
The king of the south is identified as Egypt. The robbers of the people are identified as Amalek in the land of Israel, exalting themselves as the Jews and claiming the land and the identity of God's people.

The effort to establish the vision is connected to the preceding discussion of Christian Zionist pastors, influence, and advocacy for the state of Israel. The conclusion rests on the final words, “but they shall fall.” The prophecy is presented as the reason not to be overcome by anxiety about those campaigns.

Joining forces against God's people does not protect the alliance from being broken. The application is especially to Black and Latino pastors joining outside powers against the Israelite teaching. Their association cannot overturn what God has determined.

Counsel assembled against the people comes to nothing, and the word spoken against them does not stand, because God is with Israel. The pastors' journey to Israel is applied as an example of taking such counsel together.
God instructs his people not to walk in the way of the rebellious people around them. Shared ancestry is not a reason to follow an alliance or a course opposed to his word.

precepts.why:
Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah take counsel against Judah, seeking to breach it and install the son of Tabeal as king. God declares that their plan will not stand or come to pass.

The northern kingdom joined an outside nation against its brothers in Judah. That historical setting explains the associations and counsel in the following chapter. It is then applied to our people joining other nations against the truth today: joining hands does not make a plan prevail against God's declaration.

sense.text: The scornful rulers are applied to the pastors who have the ear of the people. Their influence in Black and brown communities explains why outside powers seek their support.

The covenant with death and agreement with hell are applied to religious leaders making an agreement with the white ruling power. Their confidence is that the coming judgment will spare them because of that agreement.

Lies become their refuge, and falsehood their hiding place. Christian Zionism and its defence of the alliance are applied to those words. The hellish condition of our people is the underlying setting; the agreement does not remove it.

The tried stone, precious corner stone, and sure foundation are Christ. He is the leader on whom trust must rest. The person who believes does not make haste to leave the truth; abandoning it exposes the absence of that settled belief.
God's judgment sweeps away the refuge of lies. The waters are destruction overflowing the hiding place. Religious falsehood and even physical bunkers cannot provide safety from that judgment.

The covenant with death is disannulled, and the agreement made in the people's hellish condition does not stand. Black and Latino people joining the white ruling power will not be shielded when the overflowing scourge passes through.

The morning-by-morning report is applied to the teaching going out day and night, seven days a week. Those resisting it are vexed by understanding what the Bible is actually saying, because it exposes the falsehood in what they follow.

The response is to teach correctly and keep moving, not remain trapped in endless arguments with people refusing the report.
The short bed and narrow covering are applied to Christianity. Just as a bed too short and a covering too narrow give no comfort, that religion cannot supply the comfort people are seeking.

The Lord's strange work is his return in anger to destroy the nations and deliver the twelve tribes who believe on him. It is strange to people who were not expecting him to act in that way, and they will be shocked by it.

Do not become mockers. Mockery strengthens the bands of the judgment already determined, and the coming consumption is destruction upon the whole earth. The warning applies to brothers and sisters hearing it, not only to distant nations.

precepts.why:
Joining hand in hand does not prevent the wicked from being punished. An alliance cannot save people from the judgment attached to their wickedness.

The seed of the righteous is delivered. That distinction answers the trust placed in the covenant of Isaiah 28: deliverance is not secured by finding a powerful wicked partner.

sense.text: The wine cup of God's fury is a metaphor for the prophecy Jeremiah must deliver to the nations. Making them drink means declaring the judgment to them whether they accept it or refuse it.
The nations hear, are moved, and become angry at what is proclaimed. The sword means war. Jeremiah taking the cup and making the nations drink is his carrying out the command to prophesy.

Jerusalem and the cities of Judah are addressed first, including their kings and princes. Pharaoh and Egypt follow. Judgment begins with God's own people before the list moves through the other nations.

The mingled people are identified as Keturah's children in the Middle East. Uz is identified with modern Jordan and the Philistines with Palestine.

The map is used to connect Ashkelon with Ashqelon, Azzah with Gaza, and Ekron and Ashdod with the named places still shown in that region. The purpose is to show that the scriptural place names are not meaningless simply because modern names or spellings differ.

Edom is identified with Jordan, Moab with China, and the children of Ammon with the Japanese. Tyrus and Zidon are identified with modern Lebanon. These are the identifications used to apply Jeremiah's list to the present nations.

Dedan, Tema, Buz, and the surrounding desert peoples are connected to the Arabs. The mingled people and Zimri are connected to Keturah's children. Elam is identified with Pakistan and India, and the Medes with Iran.

The kings of the north include NATO countries such as France and Germany, with Russia also included as northward. The remaining kingdoms across the earth are covered by the wider phrase naming all the kingdoms.

Sheshach is identified as the United States of America, drinking after the others. Jeremiah 51 is used to connect Sheshach with Babylon.

The nations are commanded to drink, fall, and not rise because of the coming sword. Refusing the cup does not cancel the prophecy. Whether they accept what Jeremiah declares or reject it, they will certainly experience the judgment.

God begins with the city called by his name, Jerusalem. If he punishes his own people, the other nations cannot expect to remain unpunished. This is the force of the question, not a promise that the nations will escape while only Israel suffers.

The sword is called upon all the inhabitants of the earth. The verse is especially useful when answering the claim that God's judgment on Israel leaves the nations beyond his judgment.

Jeremiah must prophesy against all the nations named. The Lord's roar and shout announce his controversy with them. The wicked given to the sword include the nations and those among Israel who join them in opposition.

Their judgment is connected to the class's theme: liberation and good tidings for the people they oppressed. The gospel is not detached from the ending of that oppression.

Evil goes from nation to nation, and the great whirlwind is destruction with the chariots. The slain extend from one end of the earth to the other. They are not lamented, gathered, or buried, but left as dung on the ground.

The conclusion returns to the gospel as Black liberation: the end of the powers oppressing the twelve tribes is presented as the deliverance for which the people have been waiting.

precepts.why:
The verse speaks of Sheshach being taken and immediately calls the fallen power Babylon, the praise of the whole earth now an astonishment among the nations. That parallel supplies the connection between the two names.

With Babylon applied to the United States of America, Sheshach is likewise identified as America in Jeremiah 25. Its drinking after the other kingdoms is read within that application.
